title: Induced superconductivity in selective-area grown SnTe devices
authors: Maarten J. G. Kamphuis, Yoran F. S. Starmans, Pim J. H. Lueb, Femke J. Witmans, Marvin M. Jansen-Zilles, Marcel A. Verheijen, Reinoud Lavrijsen, Joost Ridderbos, Fabrizio Nichele, Floris A. Zwanenburg, Erik P. A. M. Bakkers, Alexander Brinkman
abstract: Topological superconductors are of high interest for applications in topological quantum computation. The required topologically superconducting state can be engineered by proximityinducing superconductivity in a topological insulator. Here, we explore the induced superconductivity in selective-area grown nanowires of the topological crystalline insulator SnTe on a InP substrate, through TEM/EDX and low-temperature electronic transport studies. The observed superconducting behavior likely originates from indium in the substrate diffusing upwards into the SnTe nanowire, forming a thin layer of InxSn1-xTe at the interface between the nanowire and the substrate. InxSn1-xTe is intrinsically superconducting for indium concentrations above 2%, resulting in superconductivity within the heterostructure. Little-Parks oscillations are observed in loop-shaped nanowire networks in an out-of-plane magnetic field. The half-period shift indicative of a topological superconducting state is absent, which is explained by dominant trivial transport channels obscuring any topological signatures.
summary: This paper experimentally investigates induced superconductivity in SnTe nanowires grown on InP. The authors argue that the superconductivity originates from an indium-doped interface layer ($\text{In}_x\text{Sn}_{1-x}\text{Te}$) formed by substrate diffusion. They use transport measurements, including Little-Parks oscillations, to confirm the superconducting nature and rule out other potential sources.
main_problem: The study investigates the origin of induced superconductivity in selectively area grown SnTe nanowires, aiming to determine if the superconductivity is topological or arises from interfacial doping.
main_result: The superconducting behavior is attributed to the formation of an intrinsically superconducting $\text{In}_x\text{Sn}_{1-x}\text{Te}$ layer due to indium diffusion from the InP substrate, confirming type-II superconductivity.
method: The research employed low-temperature electronic transport measurements, including differential resistance ($dV/dI$) and Little-Parks oscillation measurements in superconducting loops.
model_or_system: The physical system is a topological crystalline insulator (TCI) SnTe nanowire grown on an InP substrate. The analysis models the superconducting state using concepts like vortex flow and flux quantization ($\Phi_0 = h/2e$).
key_observables: Zero differential resistance, Little-Parks oscillations in critical current ($I_c$), and characteristic resonances in $dV/dI$ vs. current.
important_parameters: Critical temperature ($T_c \approx 350 \text{ mK}$), carrier densities ($\approx 2 \cdot 10^{20} \text{ cm}^{-3}$), and superconducting flux quantum ($\Phi_0 = h/2e$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that In diffusion forms the superconducting layer, although EDX evidence for this is limited, and the analysis notes that observed features suggest trivial bulk transport dominates over topological signatures.
figures_summary: Figures show SEM images of devices, $dV/dI$ curves confirming type-II superconductivity, and $I_c$ vs. $B$ plots demonstrating Little-Parks oscillations consistent with flux quantization.
paper_structure: The paper systematically rules out alternative sources of superconductivity (contacts, vacancies) using transport measurements (Shapiro steps, Ohmic IV curves) before confirming the superconducting nature via Little-Parks oscillations and proposing the In-diffusion mechanism as the source.
why_interesting: The work provides experimental evidence on engineering superconductivity in topological materials using proximity effects, which is highly relevant for realizing superconducting quantum circuits.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Superconductivity in SAG SnTe nanowire devices. False-colored top- view SEM images of SAG SnTe Hall bar (a) and loop (b) devices. The SnTe nanowires are colored in dark blue, the metal contacts in light blue. Also indicated schematically is the (quasi-)4-point wiring configuration for low-temperature electronic transport measure- ments. (c) Typical example of the measured differential resistance dV/dI as a function of the normalized applied current Is/Ic for both device types. A re-entrant resistance, indicative of type-II superconductivity, is observed consis- tently for all devices before the transition to the normal state.

Figure 2: Cross-sectional HAADF-STEM and EDX measurements on both device types. (a,e) HAADF-STEM cross section for the Hall-bar and AB-loop devices respectively. (b,f) Atomic resolution HAADF-STEM micrographs of the InP-SnTe interface. (c,g) EDX com- positional mappings showing the elemental distributions of In (green), Sn (red) and Al (blue). No significant intermixing of the InP and SnTe constituents can be observed. (d,h) Line profiles extracted from the white boxed area in Figures (c,g). No evidence for indium diffusion can be discerned.

Figure 3: Vortex flow channels. (a) Four-terminal longitudinal differential resis- tance dV/dI against dc-current Idc for Hall- bar device 2. Measurement taken at base- temperature (8 mK) without magnetic field. The red and blue traces correspond to posi- tive and negative sweep directions respectively. (b) The plateau resistance values in between the observed resonances of Figure a (black) and the positions of the plateaus (red). The dashed lines represent linear fittings. (c) Two- dimensional mapping of the resistance in (a) against out-of-plane magnetic field Bz. Mea- surement taken at T=50 mK.

Figure 4: Little-Parks oscillations in SnTe nanowire loops. (a-c) SEM images of three measured devices, representative of the three investigated loop sizes. (d-e) The corresponding measured differential resistance dV/dI in color scale versus magnetic field B⊥and IS. The oscil- lation frequency increases with the loop area. (g-i) Isolated oscillations in critical current against the applied magnetic field, with a subtracted background. (j) Measured oscillation frequencies versus measured effective loop area for all 8 measured devices.
